title: Start writing: the paper brief
text:
A blank page is hard; a list of questions is not. This brief asks the questions a paper has to answer, in an order that builds the outline as you go. Each answer feeds a specific paragraph, so a finished brief is a finished skeleton.
Download the brief to fill in: Word (.docx) · Markdown (.md)
How to use it:

title: Start writing: the paper brief
text:
Step 0: choose the paper type
Decide this first, because six of the questions change with the type. A regular paper answers a question about nature; a methods paper offers a way of doing something that others can reuse.









Regular paper
Methods paper




Take-home message is about
The system: species, forests, outbreaks
The procedure: how to compare, measure, forecast


Introduction ends on
A question and numbered predictions
A gap in existing methods, independent of any study system


Core of the paper
Results that answer the predictions
The method, then its evaluation


Evidence
Data from the study system
Simulations across a range of conditions, comparison with alternatives, error rates


Case study
Is the paper
One short worked example, often a single figure


Discussion
What the finding means for ecology or management
When to use the method, its limits, how to implement it



Test 1. Draft the take-home message roughly. If its subject is the system, it is a regular paper; if its subject is a procedure, it is a methods paper.
Test 2. Would the paper still matter if the case study were a different species or region? If yes, it leans methods. A good methods paper is about the method, not the study system (Ellison 2023).
If a project holds both a new method and a new finding, two papers are often clearer than one. Methods journals also set the format: at Methods in Ecology and Evolution, a Research Article (a new general method) and a Workflow (a new pipeline of existing procedures) run to 8,000 words, and an Application or Practical Tool to 4,000.

title: Start writing: the paper brief
section: Writing backwards: what it gains, what it costs
text:
Writing backwards: what it gains, what it costs
The brief starts from your results and works back to the question, following Magnusson’s “write backwards” method: conclusions first, then only the results, methods, discussion and introduction they need. It is worth using, but only with safeguards, because its main risk is quietly rewriting the question to fit the answer.









What happens
Evidence




Gain: content before style
The story is fixed first; style is easier to correct afterwards.
Expert


Gain: report what matters
You stop reporting every analysis in the order you ran it (Heard 2016).
Expert


Gain: planning improves the text
Outlining before drafting produced better documents than not outlining (Kellogg 1988).
Experimental


Gain: an easier start
You begin from what you know best: your results and figures.
Expert


Cost: HARKing
Writing the Introduction last invites presenting an unexpected finding as if it had been predicted (Kerr 1998). 51% of 807 ecologists and evolutionary biologists admitted doing so at least once (Fraser et al. 2018).
Survey


Cost: selective reporting
“Only the results the conclusions need” can slide into dropping inconvenient ones. 64% admitted not reporting non-significant results (Fraser et al. 2018).
Survey


Cost: overselling
Conclusion-first framing can push claims past the evidence.
Expert


Cost: locking in too early
Outlining improves text quality but can stop the new ideas that come from drafting, at least for some writers (Galbraith and Baaijen 2018).
Experimental, early



The brief keeps the gains and blocks the costs with five safeguards:

Record the original question first. Question C1 asks what you set out to test before you saw the results. Anything not in it is reported as exploratory.
List the results that do not fit. Question B3 has a line for them; they stay in the paper.
Calibrate claims. Each conclusion carries the hedge its evidence needs.
Leave room to discover. If you cannot answer B1 yet, write a rough discussion freely first, outline what you wrote, then return to the brief.
Change the plan for a reason. Revise the brief when a better story appears, but only if you can say why it is better (Heard 2016).

title: Start writing: the paper brief
text:
Block A: reader and venue








#
Question
Feeds




A1
Who is the reader? Name one real person outside your subfield who should understand the paper.
How much each section spells out


A2
Target journal, article type and word limit. Paragraph budget = words ÷ 160.
Paragraph count per section


A3
Regular or methods paper (Step 0)? One line on why.
Which template and question versions



How much to spell out depends on what the reader already knows (McNamara et al. 1996), and experts misjudge what novices find hard (Hinds 1999). A named reader makes both concrete. Experimental

title: Start writing: the paper brief
text:
Block B: the answer first








#
Question
Feeds




B1
Your conclusions: at most five, one sentence each, no “however”. Methods paper: what the method does better than existing ones, with numbers.
Discussion ¶1; abstract


B2
Your figures (about five at most) and tables (about four), in the order that best tells the story. One line each: what should the reader see?
Results, one or two ¶ per figure


B3
The results each conclusion needs, with direction, size and figure. Then, separately: results that do not fit the conclusions. Methods paper: performance results (accuracy, error rates, sensitivity) and the comparison with alternatives.
Results ¶; Discussion limitations


B4
The take-home message in one sentence: not what you found, but what it changes. Leave it a day, then revise.
Last sentence of the abstract; Discussion ¶1; title


B5
The central question and its answer, in two sentences.
Introduction last ¶; Discussion ¶1



From Magnusson (conclusions, then only the results they need), Heard (figure shuffling and the two-sentence mini-summary) and Fahrig (the take-home message as an implication). Expert

title: Start writing: the paper brief
section: Block C: the question and the argument
text:
Block C: the question and the argument
Answer C1 from your notes or proposal, not from memory of the results.








#
Question
Feeds




C1
The original question and predictions, as they stood before you saw the results. Mark any that changed, and any new ones: those are reported as exploratory. Methods paper: the performance claims you set out to test.
Introduction last ¶; the order of everything after it


C2
Numbered predictions, P1, P2…, in the order the paper will answer them.
Introduction last ¶; Methods, Results and Discussion order


C3
The big question your field cares about, and your pitch: resolves a controversy · a gap that blocks a wider goal · blocks a practical problem · a model system for a wider field · a new path to a hard goal. Methods paper: the task researchers need to do, in any system.
Introduction ¶1; Discussion last ¶


C4
What the reader must know first: two to four points, each with its key references. Methods paper: how the task is done now, and where that falls short.
Introduction ¶2–4


C5
The gap and why it matters, without “no studies have” or “to increase our understanding”. Methods paper: the gap in methods, stated without your study system.
Introduction gap ¶


C6
For each prediction: the data and analysis needed, and only those. Methods paper: the method’s components and assumptions, the simulation design, the alternatives compared, the case study.
Methods ¶, in prediction order


C7
The story in three lines: And (context), But (gap), Therefore (what you did and found).
Abstract; Introduction arc



From Heard (the story summary and the five pitches), Fahrig (flow-through order), McGill (the pivotal first paragraph), Olson (And, But, Therefore) and Ellison (methods papers). Expert

title: Start writing: the paper brief
text:
Block D: meaning and limits








#
Question
Feeds




D1
For each conclusion: does it agree with, extend or contradict earlier work? Name the papers.
Discussion ¶2–5, in prediction order


D2
The limitations that could change a conclusion, and by how much. Methods paper: the method’s assumptions, and when someone should not use it.
Discussion middle, never first or last


D3
What changes for management or theory? Methods paper: how to implement it; where the code and data are.
Discussion implications ¶


D4
A working title that states the finding: short, no question mark. Methods paper: a title that says what the method does.
Title


D5
What you are leaving out, and why: not relevant, redundant, or a separate paper. Conflicting results never go here.
Supplement or another paper

title: Start writing: the paper brief
text:
Four gates before drafting

Message. B4 is one sentence, states an implication, and passes the Step 0 test. You left it a day and revised it. Your reader from A1 could repeat it.
Honesty. C1 came from your notes, not your results. Every prediction not in C1 is labelled exploratory. B3 lists the results that do not fit, and D5 hides none of them.
Order. The predictions in C2, figures in B2, analyses in C6 and comparisons in D1 all follow the same order.
Budget. The paragraph count from the tables below fits the A2 budget. If it is over, cut a prediction or move it to the supplement before writing.

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
Each level of a paper holds one thing. A paper carries one message, a section does one job, a paragraph develops one idea, and a sentence adds one new point. Plan and revise from the outside in: a perfect sentence inside a paragraph you later cut is wasted effort.
The same pattern repeats at every scale: context, then content, then conclusion. Every rule below carries a label for how strong its evidence is: Experimental Correlational Descriptive Expert. They are explained at the end.

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
The workflow

Message. Make the figures, then write the take-home message in one or two sentences. Leave it a day, then revise it.
Skeleton. Put the figures in order. Draft the five pivotal paragraphs first (see Section), then one topic sentence for every other paragraph.
Draft. Write fast and do not polish. A common order is Methods, Results, Discussion, Introduction, Abstract, Title.
Revise from the top down. Paper, sections, paragraphs, sentences, words.
Test with a reader. Someone outside your subfield restates the message in their own words.

To plan before drafting, the paper brief turns stages 1 and 2 into a list of questions.

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
Paper
Goal: the reader finishes with one message they can repeat.
Write

Write the take-home message in one sentence: what the result changes, not only what you found.
Write the story as And, But, Therefore.
Choose the three to five figures that carry the message and order them as an argument.
Keep hypotheses, predictions, analyses, results and discussion points in the same order everywhere.
Write a working title that states the finding, not the topic.

Check

Can a colleague restate the message after reading only the abstract?
Does every section serve the message? What does not goes to the supplement or out.
If the Introduction lists three predictions, do Methods, Results and Discussion follow the same three, in the same order?
Is any conclusion stronger than the results support?

Example (invented, on a mountain pine beetle forecasting topic)

And mountain pine beetle outbreaks have killed pine over large areas of western Canada, and managers must decide where to act a year in advance. But most outbreak maps describe where beetles are now, not where they will spread next. Therefore we built a model that forecasts spread one year ahead and tested it against past outbreak records.



A result
Beetle spread was lower after winters with colder minimum temperatures.


A take-home message
Forecasts of next year’s spread should weight winter minimum temperature more than current models do.


A result says what you found; a take-home message says what it changes. The same goes for titles: “Investigating the dynamics of beetle spread using a forecasting framework” names a topic, while “Cold winters slow beetle spread the following year” states a finding. Use the second kind only when your results support it.
Evidence: Expert for the steps (Fahrig; Magnusson 1996; Mensh and Kording 2017; Olson 2015). Correlational more narrative abstracts and short, result-stating titles are cited more (Hillier et al. 2016; Paiva et al. 2012). Experimental result-stating titles did not change how strongly readers believed the findings (Research Integrity and Peer Review, 2016), so they help readers find a paper rather than persuade them.

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
Section
Goal: each section does one job, and together they form an hourglass.


Hourglass shape of a paper. The Introduction narrows from broad to specific, Methods and Results stay narrow, the Discussion widens back out. Numbered pins mark the five pivotal paragraphs.

Section
Its job




Abstract
The whole story in small: context, gap, approach, main result with numbers, implication.


Introduction
From the broad problem, to what is known, to the gap, ending with the aim of this paper.


Methods
Enough to reproduce the work, in the same order as the Results.


Results
One finding per paragraph. Each paragraph opens with the finding, not the method.


Discussion
The answer first, then how it fits current knowledge, limitations, and implications.



The numbered pins are the five pivotal paragraphs (McGill 2016): (1) the big question, (2) this paper’s question, (3) the main answer, (4) back to the big question, and (5) the abstract. Draft them first; the rest fills in between.
Check

Read only the first sentence of each paragraph. Do they tell the story alone?
Does the Introduction end on exactly the question the Discussion answers, stated without methods?
Are the limitations in the middle of the Discussion? The first and last paragraphs carry the emphasis.
Does the Discussion add meaning, or repeat the Results?



Opens with the method
We fitted a generalized additive model with winter minimum temperature as a predictor of spread.


Opens with the finding
Beetles spread less after colder winters (Fig. 2). We tested this with a generalized additive model…


Evidence: Expert for structure (McGill 2016; Mensh and Kording 2017; Heard 2016). Experimental headings improve readers’ memory of a text’s topic structure (Lorch et al. 2013).

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
Paragraph
Goal: one idea, stated first, then developed, with each sentence linked to the one before.







Part
What it does




Link (optional)
A few words tying this paragraph to the last: “In contrast”, “This pattern”.


Topic sentence
The paragraph’s point, stated as a claim. Skimming first sentences should give the argument.


Support, 3–4 sentences
Evidence, reasoning, citations, figure references. Each opens with something the reader already has.


Close (optional)
What the point means, or a hand-off to the next paragraph. Not a summary.



In the 148 research papers I measured from my own reading library, a typical paragraph ran about 160 words and five to six sentences.
Example (invented numbers). Shading marks information the reader already has and what each sentence adds:

Forecasts of beetle spread need an accurate map of current infestations. These maps come mainly from annual aerial surveys. Aerial surveys, however, record trees attacked the previous year, so every forecast starts one year behind the outbreak.

Each sentence picks up what the previous one ended on, then adds one new thing at its end.
Check

Can you sum up the paragraph in one line? If you need two, split it.
Do the sentence subjects form a chain the reader can follow?
Do transitions show logic (because, however, therefore) rather than just add (moreover, additionally)?
Who reads this paragraph? In the abstract and introduction, state every link; in technical methods, specialists can fill small gaps.

Evidence: Experimental putting known information before new speeds comprehension (Haviland and Clark 1974), and how much to spell out depends on the reader’s background (McNamara et al. 1996). Expert for topic sentences (Fahrig; Heard 2016).

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
Sentence
Goal: the reader understands the sentence on the first read.







Position
What goes there




Start (topic position)
Old information: who or what the sentence is about.


Subject and verb
The character and its action, early and close together.


End (stress position)
The new, important point. Readers weight it most.



Write

Find the main character and the action.
Make them the subject and verb, close together, near the start.
Put the new, important information at the end.
Split the sentence if it carries more than one new idea.
For a result, state its direction and size, not just that groups differed.



Before
An analysis of the relationship between winter minimum temperature and the survival of overwintering larvae was performed.


After
We tested whether colder winters reduced the survival of overwintering larvae.




Before
Stand age was the strongest predictor of attack, according to our model.


After
In our model, the strongest predictor of attack was stand age.




Before
Attack rates differed between young and mature stands (Table 1).


After
Mature stands were attacked about twice as often as young stands (Table 1).


Evidence: Experimental readers recalled important ideas better when actions were verbs rather than nouns (Spyridakis and Isakson 1998) and misread passive sentences more often than active ones (Ferreira 2003). Experimental keeping linked words close lowers processing cost in controlled sentences (Gibson 1998), but in natural reading the effect appeared only at nouns (Demberg and Keller 2008): mixed. Expert for stress position (Gopen and Swan 1990; Williams and Bizup).

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
Word
Goal: each word is precise, simple, and used the same way throughout.

Choose one term per concept and keep it. Keep a term list for the paper.
Cut jargon and acronyms where you can; define the rest at first use.
Prefer concrete words: organisms, places, numbers, processes.
Match hedges to the strength of the evidence.
Cut filler.









Instead of
Write
Why




utilize
use
Same meaning, shorter.


in order to
to
Filler.


it is important to note that
(cut)
If it matters, the sentence shows it.


may potentially suggest
may suggest
One hedge, matched to the evidence. Do not cut the last one.


outbreak … epidemic … infestation
outbreak, every time
Synonyms make readers think you mean different things.


spatiotemporal dynamics
where and when beetles spread
Concrete over abstract.



Evidence: Experimental needlessly complex words lowered readers’ opinion of the writer (Oppenheimer 2006); jargon lowered processing fluency even when definitions were given (Bullock et al. 2019); hedged news stories made scientists seem more trustworthy to lay readers (Jensen 2008). Correlational more jargon in titles and abstracts went with fewer citations (Martínez and Mammola 2021). Descriptive 79% of acronyms in the literature are used fewer than ten times (Barnett and Doubleday 2020).

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
How big is each part?
Count the jobs first, then check the length. The sizes below are what is typical in the papers I read, not targets.

Introduction~1,000 words · 18%5–7 paragraphs
Methods~1,600 words · 30%7–15 paragraphs
Results~900 words · 18%5–10 paragraphs
Discussion~1,600 words · 30%7–12 paragraphs

Widths show each section’s median share of the text; each small box is one paragraph at the median; ranges are the middle half of papers. Descriptive

Count the jobs. One paragraph per question, prediction, analysis or finding.
Check the budget. Paragraphs ≈ section words ÷ 160.
Check each paragraph. Over about 250 words, it probably holds two ideas. Under about 60 words, merge it or develop it.








Section
Paragraph slots, in order




Introduction
Big question (1) · what is known (2–4) · the gap (1) · question and numbered predictions (1)


Methods
Overview · one per data source · one per model or measurement · one per analysis, in prediction order · software and code


Results
Optional data overview · one or two per finding, finding first, in prediction order


Discussion
The answer · one or two per finding · limitations (in the middle) · implications · back to the big question



A methods paper has different slots; the paper brief gives both versions.
Where these numbers come from. A script read the PDFs in my Zotero library, found the four section headings, and split each section into paragraphs from the page layout. It kept 148 research papers, mostly in forest insect ecology. Tables and captions were left out, so Results look shorter than they are, and the Discussion includes any Conclusions section.

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
The practice loop
Guides describe good writing; getting better at it takes practice. Work on one skill at a time, with quick feedback and repetition (Kellogg 2008).


The practice loop: pick one skill, study a model, rewrite your own passage, get quick feedback, log the pattern, then start again.






1 · Pick one skill
2 · Study a model
3 · Rewrite yours
4 · Quick feedback
5 · Log the pattern
One skillper session



Pick one skill from your recurring problems: stress position, topic sentences, hidden verbs.
Study a model: a short passage from a well-written paper that does it well, with what it does named.
Rewrite a passage of your own applying that one skill.
Get quick feedback on that skill only, then do one more round.
Log the pattern in a personal style guide when a habit is fixed or keeps returning.

Evidence: studying models and sentence combining both improved writing in a meta-analysis of school students, so their transfer to research writing is assumed (Graham and Perin 2007). Peer feedback improved writing quality across 60 studies (Wei and Liu 2024). No schedule is prescribed: writing every day is not shown to beat other routines (Sword 2016).

title: Writing a paper, level by level
text:
How strong is this advice?








Label
Meaning
Example




Experimental
Tested by changing a text and measuring readers. Most tests used short texts and student or lay readers.
More accessible abstracts improved readers’ understanding and confidence (Freeling et al. 2021).


Correlational
Links between writing features and citations. They show associations, not causes.
More narrative abstracts were cited more (Hillier et al. 2016).


Descriptive
Trends in the literature.
Abstracts have become harder to read since 1881 (Plavén-Sigray et al. 2017).


Expert
Advice from experienced writers and editors. It rests on how readers process text but is untested.
Most of the structure above.



Readability formulas, which count word and sentence length, are not a measure of clarity: in 4,191 forestry abstracts they showed no link with citations (Jiang et al. 2026). Use sentence length only as a warning sign.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
You have a model. It has parameters. You do not know most of them exactly — you know roughly what each one could be, because somebody measured it once in a different system, or estimated it from a figure, or nobody has ever measured it at all.
So your prediction is not a number. It is a spread. Run the model across everything you might plausibly believe and the answers come out wildly different.
The question worth asking is not “what does the model predict?” It is:

Which of the numbers I don’t know is responsible for the answers coming out so differently?

That is all global sensitivity analysis is. Answer it and you know exactly which measurement would be worth making — which is the most useful thing a model can tell you before the fieldwork is done.
The worked example throughout is a winter tick–moose model with 13 uncertain parameters, analysed over 50 years.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
You have a model. It has parameters. You do not know most of them exactly — you know roughly what each one could be, because somebody measured it once in a different system, or estimated it from a figure, or nobody has ever measured it at all.
So your prediction is not a number. It is a spread. Run the model across everything you might plausibly believe and the answers come out wildly different.
The question worth asking is not “what does the model predict?” It is:

Which of the numbers I don’t know is responsible for the answers coming out so differently?

That is all global sensitivity analysis is. Answer it and you know exactly which measurement would be worth making — which is the most useful thing a model can tell you before the fieldwork is done.
The worked example throughout is a winter tick–moose model with 13 uncertain parameters, analysed over 50 years.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
section: Step 0. Why not just change one parameter at a time?

title: Global sensitivity analysis
section: Step 1. Understand what the answer will look like
text:
Step 1. Understand what the answer will look like
Before any machinery, it is worth understanding what a variance decomposition actually claims. It is simpler than the notation suggests, and you can see the whole idea in four model runs.
Two parameters, each set Low or High. Four runs, four answers. Drag the answers and watch the split change:


viewof LL = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 1, step: 0.5, label: "β low, μ low"})







viewof HL = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 9, step: 0.5, label: "β high, μ low"})







viewof LH = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 2, step: 0.5, label: "β low, μ high"})







viewof HH = Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 18, step: 0.5, label: "β high, μ high"})







sob = {
  const y = [LL, HL, LH, HH];
  const m = (LL + HL + LH + HH) / 4;
  const V = y.reduce((s, v) => s + (v - m) ** 2, 0) / 4;
  const bL = (LL + LH) / 2, bH = (HL + HH) / 2;
  const uL = (LL + HL) / 2, uH = (LH + HH) / 2;
  const Vb = ((bL - m) ** 2 + (bH - m) ** 2) / 2;
  const Vu = ((uL - m) ** 2 + (uH - m) ** 2) / 2;
  const Vs = Math.max(0, V - Vb - Vu);
  return {
    V: V, bL: bL, bH: bH, uL: uL, uH: uH,
    beta:   V > 0 ? Vb / V : 0,
    mu:     V > 0 ? Vu / V : 0,
    shared: V > 0 ? Vs / V : 0,
    effLo: HL - LL,
    effHi: HH - LH
  };
}







Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 150,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Share of the spread →", domain: [0, 1], grid: true,
      tickFormat: d => Math.round(d * 100) + "%"},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {
    domain: ["β alone", "μ alone", "shared"],
    range: ["#2c6e63", "#7a9e6b", "#b9b4a8"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(
      [{p: "β alone", v: sob.beta}, {p: "μ alone", v: sob.mu},
       {p: "shared", v: sob.shared}],
      {x: "v", fill: "p", y: () => "", sort: null}
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})







html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0.9rem 0; font-size:0.95rem;">${
  sob.V === 0
    ? "All four answers are the same, so there is no spread to divide."
    : Math.abs(sob.effHi - sob.effLo) < 0.5
      ? `β lifts the answer by <b>${sob.effLo}</b> whether μ is low or high. Its
         effect does not depend on μ, so <b>the shared piece is zero</b> and the
         two totals add to exactly 1.`
      : `β lifts the answer by <b>${sob.effLo}</b> when μ is low, but by
         <b>${sob.effHi}</b> when μ is high. That inconsistency is the shared
         piece — it belongs to neither parameter on its own.`
}</p>`







Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 720),
  height: 190,
  marginLeft: 70,
  marginTop: 30,
  marginBottom: 50,
  style: {fontSize: "13px", background: "transparent"},
  x: {label: "Total index →", grid: true},
  y: {label: null},
  color: {
    domain: ["on its own", "via interaction"],
    range: ["#2c6e63", "#d6d2c6"],
    legend: true
  },
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(
      [{p: "β", part: "on its own", v: sob.beta},
       {p: "β", part: "via interaction", v: sob.shared},
       {p: "μ", part: "on its own", v: sob.mu},
       {p: "μ", part: "via interaction", v: sob.shared}],
      {x: "v", y: "p", fill: "part", sort: null}
    ),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
})







html`<p style="margin:0.4rem 0 0 0; font-size:0.95rem;">
Totals add to <b>${(sob.beta + sob.mu + 2 * sob.shared).toFixed(3)}</b>.
${sob.shared > 0.005
  ? "They exceed 1 because the shared piece is counted in both parameters' totals — it genuinely belongs to both."
  : "With no interaction, they add to exactly 1."}
</p>`

Total spread (variance) = 46.25.
\beta’s own piece. Average when \beta is low = 1.5, when high = 13.5. Far apart, so \beta’s piece is 36.0 — that is 77.8% of the spread.
\mu’s own piece. Average when low = 5.0, when high = 10.0. Closer, so \mu’s piece is 6.25 — 13.5%.
Left over: 4.0, or 8.6%. This is the shared piece, and here is why it exists: \beta lifts the answer by 8 when \mu is low, but by 16 when \mu is high. \beta’s effect depends on \mu. That inconsistency cannot be credited to either one alone, so it gets a piece of its own.

77.8\% + 13.5\% + 8.6\% = 100\%

Exactly. Nothing lost, nothing double counted. There is only one way to do this split and it always adds up — that exactness is the point.






The one sentence to remember



How much the average answer moves when you learn a parameter’s value is that parameter’s piece of the spread. We cannot rerun history with \beta held fixed, so instead we compare the average over every run where \beta was low against the average over every run where it was high.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
Step 2. The formal version
That four-run split generalises. For a model Y = f(X_1, \dots, X_p) with independent inputs, the output variance decomposes uniquely:

V(Y) = \sum_i V_i + \sum_{i<j} V_{ij} + \sum_{i<j<l} V_{ijl} + \dots + V_{12\dots p}


V_i — variance explained by X_i on its own
V_{ij} — the extra variance from X_i and X_j acting together, beyond their separate effects
and so on for higher orders.

Divide through by V(Y) and every term becomes a share summing to 1. This is the Sobol decomposition — three plain words wearing a disguise. Variance is just how spread out the answers are. Decomposition is cutting that spread into pieces. Sobol is a person’s name (Ilya Sobol, who worked it out) and carries no meaning at all.

The two indices you report
First-order index

S_i = \frac{V_i}{V(Y)}

The share of variance explained by X_i alone. Equivalently: the fraction of uncertainty you would eliminate by learning X_i exactly.
Total index

S_{T_i} = \frac{\sum_{\text{all terms containing } X_i} V_{\dots}}{V(Y)}

X_i alone plus everything it does through interactions. Equivalently: the uncertainty that would remain if you learned every parameter except X_i.
Three diagnostics fall straight out:







Reading
Meaning




S_{T_i} - S_i
how much of this parameter’s influence runs through interactions


\sum_i S_i \approx 1
model is additive; parameters act independently


\sum_i S_{T_i} \gg 1
strong interactions; the same variance is attributed to several parameters because it belongs to none of them alone


S_{T_i} \approx 0
genuinely negligible — safe to fix and drop from the analysis



Variance is the right currency because it is model-free: no assumption of linearity, monotonicity or additivity. Compare a correlation coefficient, which only sees monotonic trends. In our run \mu_E showed a large Sobol index but a near-zero Spearman correlation, because its effect is hump-shaped. A correlation-based method would have declared it unimportant.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
Step 3. Choose the parameter ranges
This is the step with the least mathematics and by far the most consequence.
Every index is conditional on the ranges. A parameter given a wide range will tend to look important; the same parameter pinned to a narrow range will look irrelevant. This is not a flaw — it is correct behaviour, because the question being asked is “given what we don’t know, what drives the uncertainty in our prediction?” A parameter you know precisely should rank low, even if the model is mechanistically very sensitive to it.
What that meant in our case:

log10_beta_M spans three decades because nobody has ever measured it. It came out top. That ranking is a statement about our ignorance, not purely about the biology.
lambda spans ±40% because Drew & Samuel counted eggs directly. It ranked low partly because we know it well.
mu_E’s two endpoints are the two competing readings of the same paper, so its index measures what the unresolved argument costs us.







Always report the ranges next to the indices



An index without its range is not interpretable. A parameter can score low for three completely different reasons — we know it well, it genuinely does nothing, or it cannot do anything however wide the range. Those are three different findings. Say which one you mean.


Three practical rules that made the ranges defensible:
Set ranges on the interpretable quantity, then invert. We set the virulence \alpha_M by asking “how many ticks kill half a moose?” and solving

\alpha = \frac{\ln 2}{\text{burden} \times \tau_A}

Nobody can eyeball whether 2 \times 10^{-7} is sensible. Everybody can judge 38,000 ticks.
Sample on a log scale when a range spans decades, otherwise 90% of your draws land in the top decade.
Make ranges track the model’s structure. Our beta_for() helper derives \beta’s range from the current host numbers, because what matters is \beta \times \text{hosts}, never \beta alone.
Where nothing is measured at all, bound it by something you do know. Winter tick is established in Yukon, so R_0 > 1; it is at its northern range edge, so R_0 is not enormous. We set \beta_M’s range to the values putting R_0 between roughly 1 and 70. Indirect, but a real constraint and far better than three arbitrary decades.
rng_dyn2 <- list(
  # beta_M: never measured. Bounded so R0 runs from ~1 to ~67.
  log10_beta_M  = c(-7.3, -4.7),

  # mu_E: egg + free-living larval mortality, from egg-to-questing
  # survival of 30% down to 2%:  mu_E = -log(survival) / tau_E
  mu_E          = c(0.01003, 0.03260),

  # mu_N: attached nymph mortality, nymph-to-adult survival 50% to 10%
  mu_N          = c(0.00420, 0.01396),

  lambda        = c(1500, 5000),      # eggs per surviving female

  # Stage durations: the climate levers. Arthropod development runs
  # 2-3x faster per 10 C, and Yukon is projected 4-6 C warmer.
  tau_E         = c(75, 180),
  tau_Q         = c(30, 120),
  tau_A         = c(140, 200),

  M0            = c(500, 6000),       # host abundance
  U0            = c(100, 6000),

  # alpha_M: set as the burden that kills half a moose, then inverted
  #   150,000 ticks -> log10 = -7.29  (tolerant)
  #     5,000 ticks -> log10 = -5.81  (vulnerable)
  log10_alpha_M = c(-7.29, -5.81),

  k             = c(0.02, 1.00),      # aggregation; small = more clumped
  rho_M         = c(1.00, 1.20),      # moose finite rate of increase
  rho_U         = c(1.00, 1.35)
)

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
Step 4. Choose the design
You need parameter sets that cover the space efficiently. The options, with cost for p parameters:



Design
Cost
Analysis it supports




Full factorial, L levels
L^p
ANOVA


Fractional factorial
L^{p-k}
ANOVA


eFAST (fast99)
n \cdot p
Fourier decomposition


Sobol Monte Carlo
n(p+2)
Sobol estimators


Morris
r(p+1)
screening only — ranks, no quantities


Latin hypercube
n
PRCC, regression — not ANOVA



We used eFAST, for three reasons:

A full factorial at 3 levels samples each parameter at only three points. Our output spans about 10 orders of magnitude, and three points cannot describe a surface that curved. The curvature you miss gets misattributed as “interaction”.
eFAST samples continuously along space-filling curves, so it handles nonlinearity properly.
Cost is linear in the number of parameters. Going from 7 to 13 parameters cost us 2,100 → 3,900 runs instead of 2,187 → 1.6 million.


How eFAST samples
Every parameter gets its own frequency, and the design walks a single curve through parameter space. As a scalar s advances, each parameter oscillates:

X_i(s) = G_i\big(\sin(\omega_i s)\big)

where \omega_i is parameter i’s distinct frequency and G_i is the transform making X_i uniform over its range.
That sounds like a strange thing to do. Here is the trick: because each parameter wiggles at a different rate, the model’s answer wiggles back at that same rate. Take the Fourier spectrum of the output, and the power sitting at parameter i’s frequency is V_i. It is the same idea as picking one instrument out of a recording because you know its pitch. No fitting, no guessing.






Why LHS does not work with ANOVA



multisensi’s default engine is ANOVA, which needs each factor to take a few repeated levels so there are residual degrees of freedom. A continuous Latin hypercube gives every factor n distinct values, the model is saturated, and the decomposition fails. LHS is a perfectly good design — but pair it with PRCC or regression, not ANOVA.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
Step 5. Run the model
run_design(X, years = 50, out_var = "M")
takes the design table and returns:
IN   3900 rows (parameter sets)  x  13 columns (parameters)
OUT  3900 rows (parameter sets)  x  51 columns (years)
Row i out is the trajectory produced by row i in. Note the output is multivariate — 51 numbers per run, not one. That is what the next step is for.






Analyse the log when the process is multiplicative



Our tick population is multiplicative — each year is last year times a growth factor — so over 50 years small parameter differences compound into orders of magnitude. On a raw scale the variance is then owned by the handful of runs that exploded, no single parameter explains the level (because the level is a product of all of them), first-order indices collapse to nearly zero, and everything piles into interaction.
Taking logs turns that product into a sum, which is exactly the additive structure a variance decomposition is built for, and the main effects reappear. Host populations vary far less, so they don’t need it.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
section: Step 6. Reduce the output with PCA
text:
Step 6. Reduce the output with PCA
We have 51 outputs, one per year. We could run 51 separate sensitivity analyses and get 51 sets of indices. Two reasons not to:

It is unreadable. 13 parameters × 51 years × 2 index types = 1,326 numbers. There is no ranking in there a person can act on.
The outputs are massively redundant. Year 30 and year 31 are almost the same number. Naively averaging 51 sets of indices would count the same information dozens of times over.

PCA finds a small set of orthogonal shapes that trajectories vary along. Instead of 51 correlated numbers per run, each run is described by a handful of uncorrelated component scores. In our run:








Component
Variance explained
What it represents




PC1
75.4%
the overall level — how high or low the herd sits


PC2
14.2%
the transient shape — early crash and partial recovery


PC3
3.8%
early oscillation


PC4
2.6%
negligible



Three components carry 93.4% of everything that varies between trajectories.

Why orthogonality is the whole point
This is the part usually glossed over, and it is the reason the PCA is there at all. PCA components are uncorrelated by construction, which means the total variance splits additively across them:

V(\text{trajectories}) = \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 + \lambda_3 + \dots

Because there is no overlap between components, you may analyse each one separately and then combine the results by a weighted sum without double counting. If the components were correlated — as the 51 yearly outputs are — that combination step would be invalid.
So the PCA is not cosmetic dimension reduction. It is what makes Step 8 mathematically legitimate.
There is an interpretation bonus too. Each component has a temporal loading profile showing how it weights each year, so you are no longer decomposing variance “at year 37” — you are decomposing variance in trajectory shape. Asking which parameters drive the overall level, and which drive the transient, is a better question than asking about any single year.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
Step 7. Decompose the variance
Each component’s scores are one number per run, so this is now an ordinary scalar problem. eFAST estimates the decomposition from the Fourier spectrum:








Index
How it is read off the spectrum
Plain English




S_i
power at \omega_i and its harmonics
learn this one number and this much guesswork goes away


S_{T_i}
1 - V_{\sim i}/V: everything except the other parameters’ frequencies
learn all the others but not this one, and this much guesswork is left



Because it reads variance off a spectrum rather than fitting a model, there is no residual term. Nothing is left over.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
section: Step 8. Aggregate to one number per parameter
text:
Step 8. Aggregate to one number per parameter
Steps 6 and 7 give indices per component. To get one number per parameter, use the Generalised Sensitivity Index (Lamboni et al.) — the inertia-weighted average:

\text{GSI}_i = \frac{\sum_c \lambda_c \, S_{ic}}{\sum_c \lambda_c}

where S_{ic} is the index of parameter i on component c and \lambda_c is that component’s eigenvalue. Components are weighted by how much trajectory variation they actually explain, so PC1 at 75.4% dominates and PC3 at 3.8% barely contributes.
This weighted sum is only valid because the components are orthogonal. That is the payoff from Step 6. Averaging the 51 raw yearly indices instead would count the same information dozens of times over.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
The whole thing in R
library(multisensi)

gsa_time <- multisensi(
  design        = fast99,               # 1. how the sample is built
  model         = run_design,           # 2. run the model on every row
  reduction     = basis.ACP,            # 3. PCA the 51 yearly outputs
  scale         = FALSE,                #    covariance, not correlation
  design.args   = list(
    factors = names(parameters_range),
    n       = 1000,                     # runs per parameter
    q       = "qunif",
    q.arg   = lapply(parameters_range,
                     function(r) list(min = r[1], max = r[2]))
  ),
  analysis      = analysis.sensitivity, # 4. decompose the variance
  analysis.args = list(keep.outputs = FALSE)
)

summary(gsa_time)
What comes back:







Object
Contents




gsa$L
loadings — the shape over time of each component, length 51


gsa$H
scores — one per run, how strongly that run shows the shape


gsa$lambda
eigenvalues, the variance of each component


gsa$mSI
first-order indices S_i


gsa$tSI
total indices S_{T_i}



scale = FALSE means PCA on the covariance, not the correlation matrix. That is correct here because all 51 columns are the same quantity in the same units — standardising would give a quiet year the same weight as a year of collapse.






design = fast99 means this is not ANOVA



design = fast99 with analysis = analysis.sensitivity is the eFAST route. ANOVA (analysis.anoasg) is the other engine, used when you pass discrete levels through design.args instead of ranges. They estimate the same quantity by different means — see the comparison at the end.

Totals sum to about 2.4, not 1. The model is strongly non-additive. The practical consequence is blunt: “increasing X does Y to moose” is not a sentence this model supports without stating what the other parameters are doing. Any single-parameter policy claim needs a caveat.
A big gap between S_i and S_{T_i} means context-dependent. log10_alpha_M has a first-order index of 0.005 and a total of 0.16 — on its own it does essentially nothing, but it matters in combination. Virulence only bites once attachment has already put enough ticks on the animal.
A small gap means the parameter acts independently. k at 0.26 / 0.41 has the most autonomous effect in the model.
Indices are unsigned. They tell you how much, never which way. Direction has to come from somewhere else — a scatter of output against each parameter, or PRCC on a random or LHS sample. This matters: rho_U turned out negative (more alternative hosts → fewer moose), which no sensitivity index would have told us.

What to do with the answer

Measure the top-ranked uncertain parameter. beta_M at 0.80 total, with no empirical basis at all. That is the highest-value fieldwork in the system.
Settle cheap disputes. mu_E at 0.42 comes down to one sentence in a 1986 paper.
Fix and forget the negligible ones. Anything with S_{T_i} \approx 0 can be pinned at its baseline in future work.
Report ranges alongside indices. Always.

title: Global sensitivity analysis
text:
Pitfalls
Indices are conditional on the ranges. beta_M was allowed three decades; rho_M was allowed 12%. Some of beta’s dominance is that, and you must say so.
eFAST assumes independent inputs. We have a live violation: mu_E and mu_N are the same disputed reading of the same paper. If one value is right, the other almost certainly is too — so the sweep explores combinations that cannot both be true, while the indices are computed as though the two are independent. State this in the methods rather than hoping nobody notices.
eFAST cannot warn you when it fails. It has no residual by construction. If n is too small or frequencies interfere, you get plausible-looking numbers with no signal that anything went wrong. ANOVA’s residual is a feature — a built-in confession that “27% of this I could not explain”.
The trade-off runs opposite to intuition:




eFAST
ANOVA




Functional form
agnostic
limited by grid and formula order


Cost
n \cdot p
L^p


Warns you when it fails
no
yes — the residual



Both engines estimate the same Sobol decomposition. They differ in the estimator, not the target. Which is the argument for running both on a small subset once and checking they agree:
top6 <- c("log10_beta_M", "mu_E", "k", "rho_M", "lambda", "log10_alpha_M")
a <- run_gsa_dyn(as_levels(rng_dyn2[top6]))   # ANOVA, has a residual
b <- run_gsa_dyn(rng_dyn2[top6])              # eFAST, does not
plot_gsi(a); plot_gsi(b)                      # same ranking?
Watch for near-zero variance. Indices summing above 1 in the early years of our run were exactly this: tiny variance plus a finite sample gives noisy estimates.
Different questions need different analyses. R_0 cannot rank alpha_M, k, rho_M or rho_U — they do not appear in it, because R_0 is a low-density quantity. Establishment and host collapse are different questions.

text:

Lamboni, M., Monod, H. & Makowski, D. (2011). Multivariate sensitivity analysis to measure global contribution of input factors in dynamic models. Reliability Engineering & System Safety. The GSI.
Marino, S. et al. (2008). A methodology for performing global uncertainty and sensitivity analysis in systems biology. Journal of Theoretical Biology. The LHS/PRCC route, widely used in epidemiology.

title: Logistic growth
text:
The simplest population model says each individual contributes offspring at a constant per-capita rate r:

\frac{dN}{dt} = rN

which gives N(t) = N_0 e^{rt}. This is a fine description of a population that has just arrived somewhere empty, and a terrible description of one that has been there a while — it predicts unbounded growth forever.
The fix is to let the per-capita growth rate decline as the population fills up. The logistic model makes that decline linear:

\frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt} = r\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)

Read the right-hand side as the correction term it is. When N \ll K, the bracket is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential. When N = K, the bracket is zero and growth stops. When N > K, the bracket is negative and the population declines. The parameter K — the carrying capacity — is the density at which births exactly balance deaths.
Rearranged, this is the form you’ll usually see:

\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)

title: Logistic growth
text:
The simplest population model says each individual contributes offspring at a constant per-capita rate r:

\frac{dN}{dt} = rN

which gives N(t) = N_0 e^{rt}. This is a fine description of a population that has just arrived somewhere empty, and a terrible description of one that has been there a while — it predicts unbounded growth forever.
The fix is to let the per-capita growth rate decline as the population fills up. The logistic model makes that decline linear:

\frac{1}{N}\frac{dN}{dt} = r\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)

Read the right-hand side as the correction term it is. When N \ll K, the bracket is close to 1 and growth is nearly exponential. When N = K, the bracket is zero and growth stops. When N > K, the bracket is negative and the population declines. The parameter K — the carrying capacity — is the density at which births exactly balance deaths.
Rearranged, this is the form you’ll usually see:

\frac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(1 - \frac{N}{K}\right)

title: Logistic growth
Logistic growth
text:
Where the growth rate peaks
That third point falls straight out of the model. The growth rate dN/dt is a quadratic in N:

\frac{dN}{dt} = rN - \frac{r}{K}N^2

Differentiate with respect to N and set to zero:

\frac{d}{dN}\left(\frac{dN}{dt}\right) = r - \frac{2r}{K}N = 0
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
N^* = \frac{K}{2}

so the maximum growth rate is r K / 4, achieved at half carrying capacity.

title: Logistic growth
text:
Stability
The model has two equilibria, where dN/dt = 0: extinction at N = 0 and the carrying capacity at N = K. To classify them, evaluate the derivative of f(N) = rN(1 - N/K):

f'(N) = r - \frac{2r}{K}N

At N = 0: f'(0) = r > 0, so extinction is unstable — a small population grows away from zero. At N = K: f'(K) = -r < 0, so the carrying capacity is stable — perturbations in either direction decay back to it, at rate r.
This is the whole qualitative story of the model, and it’s why the continuous logistic is well-behaved to the point of being boring: one attracting state, approached monotonically from anywhere.

title: Logistic growth
text:
In R
Solving it numerically is overkill given the closed form, but the numerical setup generalises to models that have no analytical solution, so it’s worth having:
library(deSolve)
library(ggplot2)

logistic <- function(t, state, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(state, parms)), {
    dN <- r * N * (1 - N / K)
    list(dN)
  })
}

out <- ode(
  y     = c(N = 10),
  times = seq(0, 40, by = 0.1),
  func  = logistic,
  parms = c(r = 0.4, K = 200)
) |> as.data.frame()

That switches the page to the knitr engine, so R and the packages used need to be installed wherever you render. Since you render locally in RStudio, that’s fine.

title: Logistic growth
text:
Assumptions worth remembering
The logistic model earns its simplicity by assuming a great deal:

Density dependence is linear. Real per-capita growth rates often decline non-linearly, and the theta-logistic model exists precisely to relax this.
No time lags. Individuals respond to current density instantly. Adding a delay to the density term is enough to generate oscillations.
No age or stage structure. Everyone reproduces identically, regardless of age or size.
No stochasticity. Both environmental variation and demographic noise are absent, which matters enormously at small N.
Closed population. No immigration or emigration.
Constant environment. r and K don’t vary through time.

Each of these is a door to a more realistic model, and most of them are worth walking through only when the data demand it.
